nameStory: Southern arrowwood gets its name from its traditional use by Native Americans, who discovered that the young, straight stems were perfect for making arrow shafts. The wood is dense and flexible, ideal for crafting reliable arrows. The 'southern' part distinguishes it from its close cousin, northern arrowwood, though their ranges overlap considerably in New England.
description: Southern arrowwood is a medium-sized shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall, forming dense thickets in the understory. It's a member of the elder family and sports the classic viburnum look with opposite leaves and clusters of small white flowers that develop into dark blue berries. In fall, the foliage puts on a show with yellow to reddish colors before dropping for winter.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves with prominent, straight parallel veins running from the midrib to deeply toothed edges - run your finger along these ridged veins to feel the texture that gives leaves their strongly ribbed appearance

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flat-topped clusters of small, creamy white flowers in late spring to early summer, each tiny flower having 5 petals and a sweet, mild fragrance

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small blue berries in late summer that are actually drupes (like tiny plums) - they feel firm when ripe and contain a single hard seed inside

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray-brown bark on older stems that develops shallow grooves, while young stems are notably straight and flexible when bent

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, upright shrub colonies through root suckers, creating thickets with multiple stems rising from the ground rather than a single trunk

habitat: Look for southern arrowwood in mixed woodlands, especially in upland areas and along woodland edges where it gets partial sun. It thrives in moist but well-drained soils and is commonly found in oak-pine woods, hardwood forests, and floodplains throughout New England. You'll often spot it growing alongside other understory shrubs like elderberry and native roses.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with their distinctive parallel veining clearly visible, followed by flat clusters of small white flowers in late spring that attract various pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Green foliage is at its peak, and small blue berries begin developing from the flower clusters, ripening by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn beautiful shades of yellow to reddish-orange before dropping, while the blue berries become most prominent and provide food for migrating birds.
seasonality.winter: Bare stems show the opposite branching pattern and smooth gray bark, with some dried berry clusters occasionally persisting into early winter.

funFact: The blue berries contain an impressive 41% fat content, making them incredibly energy-rich for birds - that's higher than many nuts! This high fat content is why southern arrowwood berries are such an important food source for birds preparing for migration.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with northern arrowwood, which looks nearly identical but has slightly different leaf shapes and pubescence patterns. The easiest way to tell them apart is location - if you're in southern New England, you're more likely seeing southern arrowwood, while northern arrowwood dominates further north.
contextualKnowledge: There's ongoing debate among botanists about whether northern and southern arrowwood should be considered separate species or variations of the same species, as they intergrade where their ranges overlap. What's sold in nurseries as 'arrowwood viburnum' could be either species.
compareHints: Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins. It's more upright than the sprawling hobblebush and forms denser thickets than the more scattered mapleleaf viburnum. The straight, flexible young stems also distinguish it from other viburnums in the region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
